items.prompt: assertRefundAllowed's third parameter is named capturedAmountMinor. What value does the refund service actually pass in that slot?
items.answer: The remaining refundable amount, amountMinor minus the SUCCEEDED refunds
distractors: The original captured amount, Payment.amountMinor, unchanged by earlier refunds
The sum of every refund row on the payment, with PENDING rows included
The amount the operator typed into the refund form, re-validated by Zod
items.explanation: Line 33 computes remainingRefundableAmount = payment.amountMinor - refundedAmount and passes it on line 34; the guide calls the parameter name misleading for exactly this reason.

items.prompt: A FAILED payment of 100 receives a refund request for 500. Which error code comes back?
items.answer: PAYMENT_NOT_REFUNDABLE, because the status check runs before the amount check
distractors: REFUND_AMOUNT_EXCEEDS_CAPTURE, because 500 is the larger of the two violations
INVALID_PAYMENT_TRANSITION, because the refund is checked as a transition first
Both codes together, collected into error.details as a list of violations
items.explanation: assertRefundAllowed throws on the first failing check; status (lines 55-57) is tested before amount (lines 60-62), so the amount is never examined.

items.prompt: During one successful createRefundForPayment call, which statuses does the new Refund row hold, and when?
items.answer: PENDING when created, then SUCCEEDED later in the same transaction
distractors: SUCCEEDED from the start, as the simulated provider never fails
PENDING until a provider webhook arrives and marks it SUCCEEDED
PENDING, then REFUNDED once the payment total has been covered
items.explanation: createRefund writes status: RefundStatus.PENDING; after the REFUND_REQUESTED event the service calls transitionRefundStatus(refund.id, RefundStatus.SUCCEEDED, providerRefundId, tx), all inside the one prisma.$transaction.

items.prompt: You add SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the payment row at the start of the transaction. Two concurrent 40-unit refunds hit a 100 payment with 60 refunded. What does the second request receive?
items.answer: 409 PAYMENT_NOT_REFUNDABLE: after waiting it sees the first refund flipped it to REFUNDED
distractors: 409 REFUND_AMOUNT_EXCEEDS_CAPTURE: after waiting it sees a refunded total of 100 against 100
200: the lock only orders the two requests and never changes what the check sees
A deadlock error: both transactions try to lock the same payment row at once
items.explanation: The first request fully refunds the payment and sets status REFUNDED; B's read waits, then sees REFUNDED, and status is checked before amount.

items.prompt: Same row lock in place, but now two concurrent 20-unit refunds arrive against a 100 payment with 70 already refunded. Why does the second one fail with REFUND_AMOUNT_EXCEEDS_CAPTURE rather than PAYMENT_NOT_REFUNDABLE?
items.answer: A's refund was partial, so the payment stays SUCCEEDED and B fails on amount (20 > 10)
distractors: The lock is released before the status check runs, so B does not see A's committed write
Partial refunds set status PARTIALLY_REFUNDED, and that status skips the status check
Two requests queued on a lock run the amount check before the status check
items.explanation: Only a full refund flips the payment to REFUNDED (refundService.ts:64-75); after A the total is 90 with status SUCCEEDED, so B reaches the amount check.

items.prompt: In a real integration where the provider confirms refunds asynchronously, why would the current aggregate let two operators each refund the full balance?
items.answer: The sum counts only SUCCEEDED refunds, so a PENDING refund reserves no money
distractors: The refunded sum is cached per operator session, so it goes stale
PENDING refunds are deleted when the provider is slow, which frees the balance
The aggregate runs outside the transaction, so it cannot see newly inserted rows
items.explanation: sumSuccessfulRefundsForPayment filters status: SUCCEEDED; today the window is tiny only because the refund is flipped to SUCCEEDED in the same transaction.

items.prompt: An operator double-clicks the refund form's submit button and the balance allows both. What happens, and what would prevent it?
items.answer: Two refunds; only an idempotency key on the refund endpoint would stop it
distractors: One refund; the transaction rejects any repeat as a duplicate write
One refund, because the refund endpoint reuses the payment's idempotency record
Both fail, because the second request sees the first's PENDING refund and aborts
items.explanation: A transaction makes one request atomic; idempotency makes a repeated request harmless. Only payment creation has an idempotency key.

items.prompt: User B sends POST /api/payments with the same Idempotency-Key and identical body that user A used earlier. What does B get?
items.answer: A replay of A's response, including A's payment id, since the key is not user-scoped
distractors: 409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED_WITH_DIFFERENT_PAYLOAD, because the user differs
A brand-new payment of its own, since each user has a separate key namespace
400 MISSING_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY, because user A's request already consumed the key
items.explanation: findIdempotencyRecord(route, key) ignores the user, and the fingerprint covers only the body, so identical bodies match and B receives A's completed response.

items.prompt: The payment endpoint requires an Idempotency-Key, yet a double-submitted create-payment form still creates two payments. Why?
items.answer: The create hook generates a fresh Idempotency-Key on every single mutation call
distractors: The server always ignores the key when the request body is byte-for-byte identical
The key is only stored after the payment commits, so both requests miss the lookup
The browser strips custom headers like Idempotency-Key from retried POSTs
items.explanation: usePaymentActions sends crypto.randomUUID() as the Idempotency-Key per mutation, so each submission looks new. A retry must carry the same key for idempotency to work.

items.prompt: An OPS user refunds 30 of a SUCCEEDED 100 payment that has nothing refunded yet. What HTTP status and paymentStatus does the response carry?
items.answer: 202, with paymentStatus SUCCEEDED since the refund is partial
distractors: 201, with paymentStatus SUCCEEDED, as a new Refund row was made
200, with paymentStatus SUCCEEDED, the jsonOk default status
204 with no body, as a refund reply carries no payment fields
items.explanation: The route returns jsonOk(result, 202). fullyRefunded is 0 + 30 === 100, which is false, so the payment is not transitioned and the result reports payment.status, still SUCCEEDED.

items.prompt: After fully refunding a SUCCEED-mode payment, reconciliation records an issue for it on every run. Which issue, and what did the refund path forget?
items.answer: STATUS_MISMATCH: the refund path never updates ProviderPayment.status
distractors: AMOUNT_MISMATCH: the refunded total is not written back to Payment.amountMinor
MISSING_WEBHOOK: refunds create no webhook delivery row for the payment
None: reconciliation skips REFUNDED payments, so no issue is recorded
items.explanation: Reconciliation maps the provider's SUCCEEDED to SUCCEEDED and compares it with the local REFUNDED, flagging a mismatch each time.

items.prompt: The webhook service marks a bad event REJECTED using tx and then rethrows. What evidence of the failed webhook survives in WebhookEvent?
items.answer: Nothing survives: the rethrow rolls back the event row and its REJECTED mark
distractors: The REJECTED row: status updates commit independently of the rethrown error
The RECEIVED row: the insert commits before the REJECTED update is attempted
Both rows: Prisma commits each statement before the callback finishes
items.explanation: Writes made with tx share the transaction's fate; only the outbound WebhookDelivery records the failure.

items.front: Three standard fixes for concurrent over-refunds under READ COMMITTED
items.back: 1) Lock the payment row first (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) so B waits for A. 2) Run at Serializable isolation and retry on serialization failure. 3) Keep a running refundedMinor on Payment and update it with a guarded atomic UPDATE ... WHERE refunded + n <= amount, treating zero rows as 409.

items.front: Why moving reads into the transaction does not solve real provider coordination
items.back: The provider refund id is generated locally (prov_ref_<uuid>) with no external call. A real provider refund can succeed after the DB transaction rolls back, or vice versa; that needs an outbox or a request-then-confirm-via-webhook design.

items.front: How jsonError maps errors, and why the refund service catches nothing
items.back: RouteError -> { error: { code, message, details } } with its status; ZodError -> 400; anything else -> logged 500. The service lets non-domain errors propagate so infrastructure failures stay distinguishable from domain refusals.

items.front: What happens when one provider event is delivered twice concurrently?
items.back: The duplicate check reads the event before the transaction, so both deliveries proceed; the second createWebhookEvent hits the providerEventId unique constraint and surfaces as a 500.

items.prompt: A SUPPORT user's admin panel calls `POST /api/admin/reconciliation/run`. Per the flow trace, what does the browser-side `fetchJson()` do with the response that actually comes back?
items.answer: It still throws, with the fallback message "Request failed." if the body is not JSON
distractors: It resolves with a null payload, since the 403 body never reached jsonError
It throws the FORBIDDEN message taken from the { error } body jsonError built
It retries the call once, because an unhandled route error comes back as 503
items.explanation: Flow-traces lines 21-22: the RouteError is thrown at guards.ts:32 outside the handler's try, so jsonError() is never reached and Next.js receives an unhandled rejection instead of the intended structured 403. In the UI, fetchJson() (apiClient.ts:24-26) still throws on the non-OK response, but its message falls back to the literal "Request failed." when the body is not JSON. It does not resolve, there is no jsonError body to read a FORBIDDEN message from, and nothing retries.

items.prompt: The shipped test `support role cannot run reconciliation` passes, yet the guard's 403 never reaches `jsonError()`. Per the testing rationale, why can't that test notice the problem?
items.answer: It calls requirePermission() directly instead of going through withRouteAuth()
distractors: It stubs jsonError, so any RouteError it sees counts as a structured 403 body
It runs only in the .mjs runtime harness, which the npm test glob never picks up
It signs in as an OPS user rather than SUPPORT, so the permission check passes
items.explanation: Testing-rationale line 6: the test calls requirePermission() directly and does not go through withRouteAuth() in src/lib/auth/guards.ts, which is why it cannot notice that the guard throws its RouteError at line 32 outside the handler's try/catch; an HTTP-harness test of the reconciliation route asserting the structured 403 body would currently fail. The test lives in tests/auth/authorization.test.ts (line 3), a .test.ts file rather than the .mjs harness, it uses the SUPPORT role, and it stubs nothing about jsonError.

items.prompt: `buildPaymentListScope()` returns `{ ownerUserId }` for a CUSTOMER, and a shipped test proves it. Why does no CUSTOMER request exercise that branch through the HTTP API today?
items.answer: The only HTTP list route requires PAYMENT_READ_ANY, which a CUSTOMER lacks
distractors: The only HTTP list route requires the ADMIN role, so OPS sessions fail too
The list route is unwrapped, so every caller gets the staff-wide {} scope
The scope helper is only invoked by detail reads, never by the list query
items.explanation: Testing-rationale line 16: the only HTTP list route today, src/app/api/admin/payments/route.ts, requires PAYMENT_READ_ANY (route.ts:6-8 wraps GET in withRouteAuth with that permission), so a CUSTOMER never reaches the scoped branch through the API. The gate is a permission, not the ADMIN role; the route is wrapped, not open; and line 14 calls buildPaymentListScope() the ownership filter for list endpoints, not a detail-only helper.

items.prompt: `tests/runtime-refund-scope.test.mjs` loads the real refundService with stubbed repositories. What does the testing rationale say about how it runs and what it proves?
items.answer: npm test's glob skips it; it proves one shared tx client, not rollback or concurrency
distractors: npm test runs it with the rest; it proves the refund row rolls back on event failure
npm test's glob skips it; it proves two concurrent refunds can no longer over-refund
npm test runs it with the rest; it proves every read and write shares one tx client
items.explanation: Testing-rationale line 26: the .mjs file is not matched by the npm test glob in package.json:10 (tests/**/*.test.ts); it runs with node --experimental-vm-modules --test. It asserts that both refund reads and every write receive the same transaction client, plus full/partial outcomes, policy refusals, missing payment and event-failure propagation, and it does not prove database rollback or concurrency behavior.

items.prompt: Which of these sits on the testing rationale's "Not tested anywhere" list, rather than among the cases the runtime refund-scope harness already covers?
items.answer: The payload-mismatch 409 and the P2002 collision branch in paymentService
distractors: The event-failure propagation out of the createRefundForPayment callback
The missing-payment refusal raised inside the createRefundForPayment flow
The policy refusals that assertRefundAllowed raises for a large refund
items.explanation: Testing-rationale line 26 lists what the runtime refund-scope harness asserts: the shared transaction client, full/partial outcomes, policy refusals, missing payment, and event-failure propagation. Lines 28-31, "Not tested anywhere", name idempotent replay, the payload-mismatch 409 and the P2002 collision branch in src/services/paymentService.ts:168-188, every reconciliation issue type, and concurrent refunds.

items.prompt: In the create-payment request lifecycle, at what point is the replayable API response snapshot persisted?
items.answer: Last, by markIdempotencyCompleted() after the provider dispatch step
distractors: First, by createIdempotencyRecord() before the payment row is inserted
Right after createPayment() inserts the PENDING row, before dispatch
Never on the server; the browser caches the 202 and resends it on retry
items.explanation: Request-lifecycle lines 7-13: findIdempotencyRecord()/createIdempotencyRecord() replay, reject, or open a new in-progress record; then the owner is resolved, createPayment() inserts the PENDING row, PAYMENT_CREATED is appended and dispatchPaymentToProvider() runs; only at step 9 does markIdempotencyCompleted() store the replayable API response snapshot, before the 202 returns (paymentService.ts:134-160, the last write in the transaction). The opening record carries no snapshot, and nothing is cached client-side.

items.prompt: An admin demotes a signed-in OPS user to SUPPORT directly in the database. Per the auth doc, when does that user's existing session lose refund permission?
items.answer: On the next request, as each request re-reads the session row and current role
distractors: Only after logout, as the role is copied into the session row at login time
When the cookie expires, as the role travels inside the signed session cookie
After a server restart, as withRouteAuth caches each user's role in memory
items.explanation: Auth-and-permissions line 26: sessions are revocable server-side; logout deletes the session row (authService.ts:37-39) and every request re-reads the row and the user's current role (session.ts:30-43 returns role: session.user.role from the freshly loaded row). So the demotion applies on the next request. The role is not frozen at login, the cookie carries only a token resolved to a row, and the guard caches nothing.

items.prompt: A request with no session cookie, a malformed JSON body and no `Idempotency-Key` hits `POST /api/payments`. Which lifecycle step runs first?
items.answer: withRouteAuth resolves the cookie session and checks PAYMENT_CREATE
distractors: The handler parses the request body with createPaymentSchema.parse()
The handler reads the Idempotency-Key header and rejects its absence
createPaymentWithIdempotency hashes the body to look up its record
items.explanation: Request-lifecycle line 4: POST is the function returned by withRouteAuth(), so it first resolves the cookie session through getSessionForRequest() and enforces Permission.PAYMENT_CREATE (guards.ts:32). Line 5: only then does the handler parse the body with createPaymentSchema.parse() and read the Idempotency-Key header; line 6 places the fingerprint and record lookup later still, inside createPaymentWithIdempotency().

items.prompt: During payment creation, which component decides who owns the new payment and rejects an owner override the caller is not allowed to make?
items.answer: resolvePaymentOwnerForCreate() in paymentAccessPolicy, called by the service
distractors: createPaymentSchema in the route, which strips owner fields during parsing
withRouteAuth() in guards.ts, which pins the owner to the session's user
createPayment() in paymentRepository, which defaults the owner on insert
items.explanation: Request-lifecycle line 8: resolvePaymentOwnerForCreate() in src/services/paymentAccessPolicy.ts decides who owns the payment and rejects unauthorized owner overrides; load-bearing-files line 33 lists paymentService as a caller of that policy module. Line 9 gives createPayment() only the insert of the PENDING row, and neither the schema nor the guard makes the ownership decision.

items.prompt: load-bearing-files names one likely junior miswrite for `src/repositories/paymentRepository.ts`. Which is it?
items.answer: Under-fetching related rows, then re-querying ad hoc in the service layer
distractors: Eagerly fetching every related row, so each payment read loads its history
Opening a fresh transaction in each query instead of accepting the caller's
Caching payment rows in memory between requests to save database trips
items.explanation: load-bearing-files lines 46-50: paymentRepository holds the authoritative payment queries used by both write and read services and is called by five services; if it were wrong, services would decide on incomplete or stale payment shapes, especially around refunds and webhook history. The named junior miswrite is to under-fetch related rows and re-query ad hoc in the service layer, the opposite of eager over-fetching; per-query transactions and in-memory caching are not what the file names.

items.prompt: Per load-bearing-files, which two files call into `src/services/webhookService.ts`?
items.answer: The provider webhook route and providerSimulatorService
distractors: The provider webhook route and the reconciliationService
The admin webhooks deliver route and the refundService
providerSimulatorService and the paymentService module
items.explanation: load-bearing-files line 12: webhookService is called by src/app/api/webhooks/provider/route.ts and src/services/providerSimulatorService.ts. The flow trace (lines 26-30) shows the admin deliver route reaching it only through providerSimulatorService.deliverPendingWebhooks(); reconciliationService, refundService and paymentService are not among its callers.

items.prompt: What does load-bearing-files say a junior engineer would likely miswrite in `src/lib/auth/guards.ts`?
items.answer: Securing the page but forgetting to secure the underlying API route
distractors: Securing the API route but forgetting the admin page that renders it
Checking the permission after the handler has already written rows
Trusting a role read from the cookie instead of the stored session
items.explanation: load-bearing-files lines 25-29: guards.ts bridges Next.js routes and pages to shared auth and permission logic, is called by most API routes and the admin pages, and if wrong would expose protected operations even though the policy layer exists. The named miswrite is securing the page and forgetting the underlying API route, not the reverse; the other two are not what the file names.

items.prompt: If `paymentAccessPolicy.ts` were wrong, where does load-bearing-files say customer data isolation would fail first, and what is the likely junior miswrite?
items.answer: At list endpoints; ownership checked in the detail route but not the list scope
distractors: At detail pages; the list query filters by owner but single reads skip it
At refund endpoints; ownership checked on reads but never before a refund write
At login; ownership checked per request but never bound into the session row
items.explanation: load-bearing-files lines 32-36: paymentAccessPolicy centralizes ownership checks and list scoping for payment visibility; if it were wrong, customer data isolation would fail first at list endpoints, and the junior miswrite is to check ownership in the detail route but not in the list query scope. A detail-first failure, the refund-write variant and the login variant are not what the file states.

items.prompt: load-bearing-files warns about one junior miswrite in `prisma/schema.prisma`. What is it, and what would it cost?
items.answer: Merging provider and local state into one table, losing reconciliation
distractors: Folding refunds into a JSON column on Payment, losing per-refund history
Leaving out the Session model, losing server-side session revocation
Keying payments by the provider's id, losing the local replay record
items.explanation: load-bearing-files lines 39-43: the schema defines payments, provider mirrors, webhooks, refunds, reconciliation and sessions, and missing uniqueness, relations or under-modeled entities would erase whole classes of correctness guarantees. The named junior miswrite is to collapse provider state and local state into one table and lose reconciliation capability; the refunds-as-JSON, missing-Session and provider-id-key variants are not what the file warns about.

items.front: w22 is not multi-tenant. The auth doc's five steps to add tenancy later without a rewrite
items.back: 1) Add tenantId to tenant-owned models (Payment, ProviderPayment, WebhookDelivery, WebhookEvent, Refund, ReconciliationIssue). 2) Extend AuthenticatedSession with tenantId. 3) Make buildPaymentListScope() return tenant and ownership filters. 4) Make every repository read of tenant-owned data scope by tenantId before business filters. 5) Add a tenant-aware permission layer beside permissions.ts so platform admins and org operators are separated.

items.front: w22's folder layers, and the reading order the architecture overview recommends
items.back: src/app: pages and HTTP entrypoints. src/components: client UI that calls React Query hooks. src/hooks: the browser data boundary that calls REST and owns cache invalidation. src/services: business logic. src/repositories: the database boundary. src/lib: cross-cutting policy and domain rules. prisma/schema.prisma: relational source of truth. Read schema, permissions.ts, paymentService, webhookService, reconciliationService: schema first, policy second, write path third, async correction paths fourth.

items.front: Which service is the primary owner of each w22 entity?
items.back: authService: User and Session. paymentService: IdempotencyRecord and Payment. providerSimulatorService: PaymentAttempt, ProviderPayment and WebhookDelivery. webhookService: WebhookEvent. refundService: Refund. reconciliationService: ReconciliationRun and ReconciliationIssue.

items.front: How w22 keeps an audit trail of each payment, and the risk if it were wrong
items.back: PaymentEvent rows are appended through one write boundary, createPaymentEvent() in paymentEventRepository, which the payment, refund, webhook and reconciliation services all call; PaymentDetailsCard renders the trail for operators. If wrong, operators lose the historical sequence needed to explain incidents or financial anomalies.

items.front: The four shipped .test.ts files: the risk each guards, and which one needs installed dependencies
items.back: SUPPORT cannot run reconciliation: a privileged action exposing system-wide financial state, so RBAC must be trustworthy. FAILED cannot move back to SUCCEEDED: terminal-state regressions create false revenue or refund eligibility. CUSTOMER list scope: list endpoints are the easiest place to leak multi-record data. Non-positive amounts rejected: amount validation belongs at the API boundary. Only the schema test imports zod; the other three import local source and node: modules.

items.front: Where w22 draws its Zod validation boundary, and what goes wrong without it
items.back: createPaymentSchema and refundPaymentSchema live in src/lib/validation/paymentSchemas.ts; the payments route and the refund route call .parse() before any business logic. Without that boundary, malformed money values or weak refund reasons reach service code and fail later in less predictable ways.

items.front: w22's staff roles: what SUPPORT, OPS and ADMIN may do, and where the map lives
items.back: src/lib/permissions.ts holds the explicit role-to-permission map. SUPPORT can read any payment but cannot create, refund, deliver webhooks or run reconciliation. OPS can create payments, read any payment, refund, deliver webhooks and run reconciliation. ADMIN has the same operational permissions as OPS.
